clue.text: They turn up orating — flashy Uber customers?

parts.note: something flashy and showy is loud, as in a loud shirt
people who hail a cab or ride are hailers; Uber is a ride-hailing app

explanation.surface: A puzzle over what to call the showy people who summon an Uber ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the stretch: an Uber is booked by app, not flagged down, but its customers are still hailing a ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Megaphones amplify a speaker's voice, so they turn up the volume of anyone orating through them.

clue.text: Spotted cat with snapping canines

parts.note: a description of the big spotted feline with sharp teeth; canines can mislead as dogs

explanation.surface: A spotted cat faces a pack of yapping dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: Almost a straight definition: canines are the cat's own pointed teeth, not dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: The big African and Asian feline with rosette spots and powerful fangs is described exactly.

clue.text: University philosophy student inclined to be hard going

parts.note: Phil is short for philosophy
L, for learner, stands for a student

explanation.surface: A philosophy undergraduate finds the course a struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inclined' hints at the slope sense too, but the definition is 'hard going'.
explanation.definitionFit: An uphill task is a difficult, laborious one, as climbing a slope is.

clue.text: Theatrical cast sit in choir

indicators.note: cast means thrown about, so these letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A dramatic cast of performers sits among the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' reads as actors, fitting 'Theatrical', but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Histrionic behaviour is melodramatic and exaggerated, as though on stage.

clue.text: More than one mischief-maker is ringing politician

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A troublemaker is phoning a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Imps are small mischievous sprites, so plural naughty children or fairies.

clue.text: Adjacent parts of steeple vane scenically fade

indicators.note: adjacent parts of the words means a run of letters across neighbouring words

explanation.surface: A weathervane on a church steeple slowly fades from the scenic view.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is to vanish gradually, to disappear like vapour.

clue.text: Like a devil or a saint gone astray, getting caught

indicators.note: gone astray means wandered off course, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A saint who strays and is caught out looks devilish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone astray' rearranges A SAINT into SATANI.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means of Satan, the chief devil, so devilish or fiendish.

clue.text: Fool's hoarding high-explosive gear

indicators.note: a thing hoarding something keeps it stored within, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a clot is a fool, and the 's makes it CLOTS
HE is the standard abbreviation for high explosive

explanation.surface: An idiot has been stockpiling dangerous explosive equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear is an informal word for garments, what one wears.

clue.text: One gets ready to come out on the street?

definitions.text: One gets ready to come out on the street?

parts.words: One gets ready to come out on the street?
parts.note: ready suggests prepared, but here it is slang for money that an ATM dispenses on the street

explanation.surface: Someone preparing to go out into the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ready' is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall-mounted ATM in a high street dispenses banknotes, the ready money.

clue.text: Vocally cool one from Cats — Lloyd Webber's work?

indicators.note: vocally means the pieces are said aloud, giving a word that sounds the same but is spelt differently

parts.note: to fan something is to cool it; a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Praise for a singer from the musical Cats as a fine Lloyd Webber creation.
explanation.walkthrough: Cats suggests the musical, but here it just means felines; Lloyd Webber also wrote The Phantom of the Opera, so the short title stands for his show, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phantom of the Opera is Andrew Lloyd Webber's best-known musical, often called simply by its first word.

clue.text: Soldier authorised to raise gun offers top covering fire

parts.note: to man is to staff; a man is an ordinary soldier

indicators.note: in a down answer, to raise is to lift the letters upward, reading them backwards

parts.note: let means allowed or authorised
a piece is slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A soldier cleared to lift his weapon gives covering fire from above.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering fire' is a military term in the surface, but the definition is the shelf above a fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantelpiece is the shelf over a fireplace, literally sitting on top of the hearth.

clue.text: Young son and cook going round arcade

indicators.note: the son and cook pair go round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: to fry is to cook
a shopping arcade is a mall

explanation.surface: A boy and a chef wander around a shopping arcade.
explanation.definitionFit: Small fry is an idiom for young children, the little ones, used as a collective noun.

clue.text: Singer that's rejected Christmas — gripping news!

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the letters are read in the other direction
gripping means holding within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Noel is Christmas
news read as plural of N, the abbreviation for new, gives two Ns

explanation.surface: A singer turns down Christmas, a gripping news story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is read as the plural of N (new), a rare but fair trick; 'gripping' makes NONNEL, which 'rejected' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lennon was the Beatles singer and songwriter, so he is an example of a vocalist.

clue.text: Short-term policies involving sheet music?

parts.note: a sheet is a cover, as on a bed
music is written in notes

explanation.surface: Temporary arrangements that include printed sheet music.
explanation.definitionFit: Cover notes are temporary insurance documents issued until the full policy arrives.

clue.text: Was the creator of cheese from the East?

indicators.note: in an across answer, reading from the east means right to left

parts.note: Edam is a Dutch cheese

explanation.surface: A question about who first made a cheese that came from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: To have made something is to have been its creator, the past tense of produce.

clue.text: My lead-free scooter managed around 150 — fast vehicle

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters go round the other piece
managed suggests letters handled and reworked into a new order
lead-free means the word loses its leading letter

parts.note: CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone boasts their unleaded scooter reached nearly 150, quite a fast ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead-free' reads like petrol, but it beheads scooter; 'managed' then rearranges the letters into MOTORYCE, which goes 'around' the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorbike is a quick powered two-wheeler, a fast vehicle.

clue.text: Disreputable dance action Americans like to watch

parts.note: base means low or dishonourable
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A seedy dance performance that appeals to American viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: The bat-and-ball game is the great American summer pastime, watched by millions.

clue.text: Pitch tent while taking in river and towers

parts.note: to pitch a tent is to camp

indicators.note: taking in means holding within, so one piece is inside the other

parts.note: as can mean while, as in 'as I walked'
the Nile is the African river

explanation.surface: Instructions to set up camp by a river with towers nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: A campanile is a free-standing bell tower, as found beside many Italian churches.

clue.text: Peter out in Ilkley, maybe more miserable

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: Ilkley Moor in Yorkshire is a moor, the subject of a famous folk song
to peter out is to fizzle and die

explanation.surface: Someone called Peter, out walking near Ilkley, perhaps getting gloomier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name but 'Peter out' is a phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Moodier means sulkier, more given to low spirits, a comparative of gloomy.

clue.text: Tramp makes dogs etc recoil

indicators.note: to recoil is to spring back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: dogs, cats and the like are pets

explanation.surface: A vagrant causes dogs and other animals to shrink back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a vagrant noun but is the verb, to tread heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk with heavy footfalls, a synonym of tread or pace.

clue.text: Bear consuming almost every bun?

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to bear something is to take it

indicators.note: almost means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: each means every

explanation.surface: A bear devours nearly every bun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal but is the verb, to endure; 'almost' docks a letter before 'consuming' does its work.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a light sweet yeast bun with currants, often toasted.

clue.text: New Age gathering united in country

indicators.note: gathering means collecting within, so the jumbled letters enclose the others
new suggests the word made fresh by rearranging its letters

explanation.surface: A New Age festival brings people together in one country.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinea is a nation in West Africa.

clue.text: After eating duck, diner's fancy decreased?

indicators.note: after eating means one piece has been swallowed into the other
fancy as a verb or adjective suggests imaginative rearrangement of letters

parts.note: the letters of diner, with 's read as 'is'
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, O

explanation.surface: A diner's appetite has fallen off after a meal of duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges DINER to IRNED, which takes O inside. The definition is read as de-creased: pressing removes creases.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes pressed with an iron have had their creases taken out, a punning reading of the definition.

clue.text: Cool shade keeps chap cold inside

parts.note: in means fashionable, cool

indicators.note: keeps means holds, so one piece lies within the other
inside confirms the chap sits within the shade

parts.note: a hue is a shade of colour
a man is a chap

explanation.surface: A cool spot of shade keeps a man from the cold indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cold and unfeeling lacks compassion, which is what cruel and heartless mean.

clue.text: Note about that fellow you employed in the past

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
he refers to that fellow

explanation.surface: A memo about a man once employed.
explanation.definitionFit: Thee is the archaic object form of the second-person pronoun, used in old texts.

clue.text: Personal account that gets carved up when one's dead?

definitions.text: Personal account that gets carved up when one's dead?

parts.words: Personal account that gets carved up when one's dead?
parts.note: carved up suggests an estate being divided, but it means words cut into a gravestone summing up a life

explanation.surface: Someone's bank account gets split among heirs after death.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombstone inscription is a brief personal record of the deceased, literally carved.

clue.text: Piggott on nag, evidently concealing weight

indicators.note: concealing means the letters lie hidden within the run of words

explanation.surface: The jockey Lester Piggott, aboard a poor horse, obviously hides his weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Lester Piggott was a famous British jockey.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonnage is the weight or carrying capacity of a ship, measured in tons.

clue.text: Big wave — something in the sea that is ridden precariously?

parts.note: a roller is a long heavy breaking wave
a skate is a flat fish found in the sea

explanation.surface: A huge wave, a thing out in the sea that surfers ride riskily.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests surfing a wave; the definition is the wheeled boot that wobbly beginners ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A boot on wheels is something one balances on and rides, often unsteadily.
